title: 8 Days in Crete: A Day-by-Day Itinerary
seoTitle: 8 Days in Crete: A Complete Day-by-Day Itinerary
seoDescription: An eight-day Crete itinerary from Chania to Heraklion — Balos, Elafonisi, the Samaria Gorge, Lake Kournas, Preveli, Rethymno and Knossos, with timings for each.
summary: Eight days is enough to cross Crete properly: three days in and around Chania for the old town, the Balos lagoon and Elafonisi, one day walking the Samaria Gorge from Omalos to Agia Roumeli, then a shift east to Rethymno for Lake Kournas and the Argyroupoli springs, the Kourtaliotiko Gorge and the Preveli palm forest, a full day in Rethymno's Venetian old town, and a final day at Knossos, the Heraklion Archaeological Museum and Heraklion city. The heaviest day is Samaria at five to seven hours of walking; the lightest is Rethymno at three to four hours on foot. Every other stop wants between two and four hours on the ground, which is why this works better as two bases — Chania for days one to four, Rethymno for days five to eight — than as one.
body:
This is the west-to-east version of Crete: three days around Chania, one long day in the Samaria Gorge, then a move east to Rethymno for water, gorges and Venetian streets, finishing with the Minoans at Knossos and Heraklion. Spring and early autumn suit it best — summer is hot for the gorge days, winter is quieter but wetter.

## The eight days at a glance

| Day | Base | Where | Time on the ground |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Chania | Chania old town and the Venetian harbour | Half a day, unhurried |
| 2 | Chania | Gramvousa and Balos Lagoon, by boat from Kissamos | 20–30 min climb to the fortress, plus 2–3 h at the lagoon |
| 3 | Chania | Elafonisi | 3–4 h |
| 4 | Chania | Samaria Gorge, Omalos to Agia Roumeli | 5–7 h walking, plus the ferry out |
| 5 | Rethymno | Lake Kournas and Argyroupoli Springs | 1.5–2 h at the lake, 2–3 h at the springs |
| 6 | Rethymno | Kourtaliotiko Gorge and Preveli Palm Forest | 2–3 h each |
| 7 | Rethymno | Rethymno old town and beach | 3–4 h walking, plus an hour on the promenade |
| 8 | Rethymno | Knossos, the Archaeological Museum and Heraklion | 2–3 h, 1–2 h and 2–3 h |

Days one to four all run out of Chania; days five to eight are easier from Rethymno, which sits about an hour from Chania airport and an hour and a half from Heraklion. Moving base once, on the evening of day four, saves several hours of driving over the week.

## Day 1 — Chania: falling for a city on foot

**In short:** an unhurried half day in the old town and around the Venetian harbour, ending with dinner by the water. No driving.

### The harbour

The first thing you notice in Chania is the calm pulse of the place: cobbled streets, the smell of bread from small bakeries, people greeting each other. The Venetian harbour is the right place to start. Boats sway in the morning light, the lighthouse stands at the edge of the water, and the cafés fill with locals over coffee. It is worth an hour of doing nothing at all.

### The old town quarters

Topanas feels like a neighbourhood frozen in time — Venetian buildings with carved balconies, small galleries and quiet tavernas behind doors you would miss if you were hurrying. Splantzia, with its shaded squares and old churches, is slower and more secretive. In the Jewish Quarter the street shapes, stone walls and small courtyards change again. Athinagora Square, with its cathedral, benches and fountain, is where to sit and let the city move around you.

### The Maritime Museum

The Firka Fortress by the harbour houses the Maritime Museum, and it rewards a slow walk: old maps, ship models and photographs that remind you Crete has always been shaped by the sea. It does not feel like a formal museum — more like a room where someone left their memories.

### Eating and drifting

A harbour-side taverna for grilled octopus, fresh sardines or *dakos* — the barley rusk salad with tomato, cheese and olive oil. Afterwards, wander without a plan: Stivanadika Street with its leather shops, hidden courtyards, vines over balconies. Return to the harbour as the light goes gold, with a glass of local wine or raki, and watch the last boats come in.

## Day 2 — Balos Lagoon and Gramvousa

**In short:** a boat from Kissamos to Gramvousa island and the Balos lagoon. Budget a 20–30 minute climb to the fortress and two to three hours at the lagoon.

### The crossing and the fortress

The roads west toward Kissamos hint at what is coming: rugged cliffs, olive groves running down to the sea, glimpses of turquoise far below. From the port a small boat crosses to Gramvousa, a rocky outcrop topped with a fortress that seems to grow out of the island. The climb is steep, uneven and takes 20 to 30 minutes depending on pace — not technically difficult, but sturdy shoes help. From the top you can see the lagoon's sandbars stretching like ribbons, the scattered islets and the cliffs of the coastline.

### The lagoon

Back down at Balos, the shallow water lets you wade far out, watching small fish move around your feet. Walking the sandbars feels almost like being suspended between sea and sky. Give it at least two hours — three if you want to find the quieter pockets and cross the narrow sandbar to the small islet.

### Practical notes

- The Gramvousa climb takes 20–30 minutes each way.
- Allow 2–3 hours at Balos to walk, wade, swim and explore without rushing.
- Bring water, sunscreen and a snack: there are very few facilities at the lagoon.
- Morning or late afternoon means fewer crowds and softer light; midday is intense.

## Day 3 — Elafonisi

**In short:** pink sand, a shallow lagoon and dunes. Three to four hours, with almost no shade.

### The beach

The drive south-west winds through mountain roads and olive groves before the pink-tinted sand comes into view — fine grains mixed with crushed shell. The water stays shallow for dozens of metres and warms in the sun, so it is walkable rather than swimmable in places, which is exactly what makes it work for anyone travelling with children.

### The islet and the quiet ends

Walking the sandbars, the lagoon stretches out like a natural pathway. Cross to the small islet connected by a narrow sandbar and the water is on both sides of you. Past the main congregation areas, hidden coves and quieter stretches of sand appear between low rocky ridges — this is where Elafonisi stops feeling crowded. Walking paths run through the surrounding dunes and low hills, with wildflowers in spring.

### Practical notes

- Allow 3–4 hours to walk the beach, cross to the islet and take breaks.
- Morning or late afternoon is ideal; the midday sun is strong and the main beach gets busy.
- Shade is limited — a small umbrella or a spot under the tamarisk trees helps.
- Comfortable sandals for the shallow lagoon and dunes.

## Day 4 — The Samaria Gorge

**In short:** the big one. An early start from the Omalos Plateau, five to seven hours of walking to Agia Roumeli, then a ferry out. There is no shortcut once you have started.

### The descent

The roads up to Omalos pass through mountains that still hold snow in spring, pine forest and valleys that look untouched. The trail begins with a descent under towering cliffs and thick vegetation, pine arching overhead, small streams of clear water alongside the path. The air smells of resin and earth, and the noise drops away to birds, leaves and your own footsteps.

### The Iron Gates

As the gorge narrows the walls rise steeply, in places more than 600 metres above you. At the Iron Gates the gorge closes almost completely — the most photographed few hundred metres in Crete, and a place where every glance upward is worth the stop. Along the trail you pass old stone huts, chapels and abandoned villages, evidence of people living alongside this landscape for centuries.

### Agia Roumeli

The walls open, the vegetation thickens, and eventually you hear the sea. The trail ends at Agia Roumeli, where the gorge spills into the Libyan Sea. Swimming there is less refreshment than rite of passage. Simple tavernas let you sit and watch boats bringing the next day's hikers in, before the ferry takes you back.

### Practical notes

- Start early: the hike is long and the sun is hard in summer.
- Allow 5–7 hours for the full walk from Omalos to Agia Roumeli.
- Sturdy shoes are essential — long sections are rocky and uneven.
- Carry plenty of water and light snacks. There are a few small shops on the trail but the options are limited.
- Spring and early autumn are the most comfortable months; summer is hot, winter is wet and cold.

## Day 5 — Lake Kournas and Argyroupoli Springs

**In short:** the recovery day after Samaria. Fresh water, shade and short walks — around two hours at the lake and up to three at the springs.

### Lake Kournas

Crete's only freshwater lake sits among rolling hills and olive groves, and it feels nothing like the coast. The water is still enough to mirror the hills, the shore is edged with reeds, small pebbly beaches and picnic areas shaded by tamarisk. A lakeside path takes you round; pedal boats let you cross it without an engine. Allow an hour and a half to two hours to see it from several angles.

### Argyroupoli Springs

A short drive brings you to Argyroupoli, where water is everywhere: small waterfalls over moss-covered rock, streams under stone bridges, fountains rising from ancient sources. Roman-era structures and old stone mills sit among the paths, and shaded tavernas serve fresh trout, Cretan cheeses and salads beside the streams. Higher trails give views over the village, the olive groves and the mountains behind. Allow two to three hours.

### Practical notes

- Lake Kournas: 1.5–2 hours for a comfortable circuit, longer if you paddle or picnic.
- Argyroupoli: 2–3 hours.
- Comfortable shoes for stone paths and small bridges.
- Most of the springs area is shaded, with tavernas for breaks.

## Day 6 — Kourtaliotiko Gorge and the Preveli Palm Forest

**In short:** a gorge with five springs in the morning, a river walk through a native palm forest to a beach in the afternoon. Two to three hours each.

### Kourtaliotiko Gorge

Cliffs rise on both sides of the road as you approach, and the air smells of wild herbs. The walk follows a lively stream between steep walls, and the highlight is a series of five natural springs — one cascading over mossy rock, another gathering in a quiet pool with small fish, another forming a waterfall that cools the air around it. Small trails branch off to secluded spots by the stream.

### The Preveli Palm Forest

A short drive leads to Preveli, where the Megalopotamos River runs down to the sea through dense stands of *Phoenix theophrasti* — the native Cretan date palm, one of the few palms indigenous to Europe. The trail follows the river past clear pools and dappled light, and you can step into the water in many places. Follow it to the small beach where the river meets the Libyan Sea and swim in either.

### Practical notes

- Kourtaliotiko: 2–3 hours to walk the gorge and take in all five springs.
- Preveli: 2–3 hours at a relaxed pace, including the river walk and a swim.
- Comfortable walking shoes — the gorge path is rocky and uneven.
- Bring water, sunscreen and swimwear if you plan to get into the river.
- Spring and early autumn are ideal; summer is hot and busy, winter cooler and much quieter.

## Day 7 — Rethymno

**In short:** the most walkable old town in Crete. Three to four hours of landmarks at a relaxed pace, plus an hour on the beach promenade.

### The Fortezza

The fortress dominates the town from its hilltop. Built by the Venetians between 1573 and 1580 to protect the city from pirate raids and Ottoman invasion, it uses the landscape cleverly — high bastions over the town and sea, thick walls shielding the interior. From the ramparts the old town spreads below, the harbour catches the light, and on clear days the mountains sit behind it all.

### The Venetian and Ottoman town

Descending into the old town you reach the Rimondi Fountain, built in 1626, in a small square shaded by trees. Nearby, the Venetian Loggia, built around 1626–1629, once hosted official gatherings and town meetings and remains remarkably well preserved. The Neratze Mosque, built in 1657 on the site of a former Venetian church, marks the Ottoman layer with its minaret and modest dome. Along the same streets stand the Church of the Virgin Mary and Saint Francis Church.

The Topanas district is a labyrinth of narrow lanes lined with Venetian houses, wooden balconies leaning over the street, courtyards hiding cafés and workshops. The Skaramangas Mansion is a fine example of 17th-century urban architecture. Arkadiou Square holds the Venetian-era Arkadiou Fountain, and Splantzia Square, shaded by plane trees, sits beside the Church of Our Lady of Angels, built in 1587 on earlier Byzantine remains.

### The beach and the late afternoon

The promenade runs alongside a wide town beach with shallow water, fishing boats in the harbour, and cafés the length of it. Then go back into the alleys in the late afternoon, when the light softens and the balconies glow — this is when Rethymno is at its best.

### Practical notes

- The main landmarks — Fortezza, Rimondi Fountain, Loggia, Neratze Mosque, Topanas, Splantzia — take about 3–4 hours at a relaxed pace with breaks.
- The beach promenade adds another hour.
- Comfortable shoes are essential: cobblestones, uneven alleys and small steps throughout.
- Early morning or late afternoon gives the best light and the quietest streets.

## Day 8 — Knossos, the Archaeological Museum and Heraklion

**In short:** the Minoan day. Two to three hours at Knossos, one to two in the museum, two to three in the city. It is a long day and a long drive from Rethymno, so start early.

### Knossos

Built between roughly 1900 and 1400 BCE, Knossos is the largest Bronze Age archaeological site on Crete, and it was not just a palace but a centre of power, religion and daily life. Walking the central courtyard, the scale is the thing: ceremonial spaces, storage, trade. The Throne Room, with its alabaster seat and wall frescoes, gives the clearest window into Minoan ritual and authority, and the frescoes — dolphins, lilies, ceremonial scenes — put colour back into the ruins. Allow two to three hours to do it properly.

### The Heraklion Archaeological Museum

A short drive away, the museum holds some of the finest Minoan artefacts anywhere: pottery, carved jewellery, ceremonial figurines and fresco fragments, including the snake goddess figurines. It is what connects the scale of Knossos to the objects the people there actually made and used. One to two hours, more if you read everything.

### Heraklion city

The streets are busy but relaxed, with cafés spilling into the squares. Walk Daedalus Street and the Morosini Fountain — the Lions Fountain — where Venetian architecture meets modern Cretan life, and stop for a *bougatsa* filled with cream or cheese. The harbour area has the old fortifications, fishing boats and a wide horizon. Two to three hours at a relaxed pace.

### Practical notes

- Knossos: 2–3 hours.
- The Archaeological Museum: 1–2 hours, more if you want to study every case.
- Heraklion streets, fountain, market and harbour: another 2–3 hours.
- Comfortable shoes and sun protection — Knossos has very little shade.
- Spring or autumn is ideal; summer is hot, winter quieter.

## Making the week easier

Three things save time on this route. Move base once rather than driving back and forth: Chania for days one to four, Rethymno for days five to eight. Put the two hardest days — Samaria and Balos — early, while legs are fresh and before the heat builds. And do not try to add Knossos to day five or six as a detour; it needs its own day, and the drive is longer than the map suggests.

faqs.a: It is enough for the western two-thirds. This itinerary covers Chania, Balos, Elafonisi, the Samaria Gorge, Lake Kournas, Argyroupoli, Kourtaliotiko, Preveli, Rethymno, Knossos and Heraklion — which is a full week without rushing, provided you change base once. It does not reach eastern Crete: Elounda, Spinalonga and the Lasithi Plateau would need extra days.

faqs.q: Where should I stay for an 8-day Crete trip?
faqs.a: Two bases. Chania for days one to four, since Balos, Elafonisi and the Omalos trailhead for Samaria are all in the west. Then Rethymno for days five to eight, which puts Lake Kournas, Argyroupoli, Kourtaliotiko and Preveli within short drives and shortens the run to Knossos on the final day.

faqs.q: How hard is the Samaria Gorge walk?
faqs.a: It takes most people five to seven hours from Omalos to Agia Roumeli, and once you have started there is no way out other than finishing. It is downhill throughout, which loads the knees, and the ground is rocky and uneven. Start early, wear sturdy shoes, and carry water — there are only a few small shops on the trail.

faqs.q: Do I need a car for this itinerary?
faqs.a: For the driving days, yes — or a guided transfer. Public transport between regions in Crete is limited and does not connect the gorges, springs and beaches on this route. Day one in Chania and day seven in Rethymno are entirely on foot, and Samaria ends with a ferry rather than a return drive.

faqs.q: What is the best time of year to do this trip?
faqs.a: Spring and early autumn. Summer is hot for the Samaria and Kourtaliotiko days and busiest at Balos and Elafonisi; winter is quiet and cool, with a real chance of rain in the gorges.

faqs.q: Can I visit Knossos and Elafonisi in the same trip?
faqs.a: Yes, but not from the same base and not on the same day. Elafonisi is in the far south-west and Knossos is just outside Heraklion, roughly the length of the island apart. This itinerary puts Elafonisi on day three from Chania and Knossos on day eight from Rethymno.

faqs.q: How much time should I allow at Balos and Elafonisi?
faqs.a: Two to three hours at Balos on top of the 20 to 30 minute climb to the Gramvousa fortress, and three to four hours at Elafonisi if you want to walk the beach and cross to the islet. Both are best in the morning or late afternoon — midday brings the crowds and the hardest light.
